stimuli.title: A station for the village
stimuli.content:
In a small town on the edge of a dry district, a radio station broadcasts from two rooms above a grocery shop. Its signal reaches only about fifteen kilometres, and most of its presenters are farmers, housewives and students who had never spoken into a microphone before. This is community radio: a low-power station run by and for the people of a small area.

Unlike large commercial channels, which try to attract as many listeners as possible across a city or a state, a community station serves a few villages and speaks in their own dialect. Its programmes are shaped by local needs. A typical day might include a talk by an agriculture officer on pest control, a call-in show on a new pension scheme, folk songs recorded at a wedding and the prices of vegetables at the nearest market.

Supporters say that the greatest strength of such stations is trust. Listeners recognise the voices on air; the person reading out a weather warning may be a neighbour's daughter. During floods and heavy storms, when mobile networks often fail, community stations have kept villages informed about rising water levels, safe shelters and relief camps.

Running a station, however, is not easy. Most are operated by schools, colleges or voluntary organisations with little money. They cannot depend on advertising, since local businesses are small and the stations are allowed to broadcast only a limited amount of it. Equipment breaks down, trained volunteers move away to cities, and licences take a long time to obtain.

Many stations have survived by involving their listeners. Villagers donate small sums, women's groups produce their own programmes, and young people learn to record and edit on cheap phones. As one station manager put it, the station does not belong to its staff; it belongs to the people who keep switching it on.

stimuli.title: Driving blind in the fog
stimuli.content:
Every winter, large parts of northern India disappear under a thick blanket of fog. For railway passengers, the season brings a familiar frustration: trains that run hours, sometimes a whole day, behind schedule. Passengers often blame poor planning, but the main cause is simple. A driver who cannot see the signal ahead cannot safely run his train at full speed.

Railway signals work much like traffic lights. A red light tells the driver to stop, while yellow and green lights tell him how much of the line ahead is clear. In good weather a driver can see a signal from a long distance and adjust his speed calmly. In dense fog, visibility may fall to a few metres, so he may not spot a red signal until it is too late. A heavy train needs a long distance to halt even after the brakes are applied. Rules therefore require trains to slow down sharply when the fog is thick.

Technology has eased the problem without removing it. Many locomotives now carry a small device that uses satellite positioning to tell the driver how far away the next signal is, and sounds an alert as the train approaches it. Drivers say this removes much of the guesswork. Some routes are also being fitted with systems that can apply the brakes automatically if a train passes a red signal or goes faster than the safe speed.

Even so, delays cannot be avoided entirely. One late train holds up the trains behind it on a busy line, and the effect spreads across the network. Railways therefore cancel or shorten some services in the foggiest weeks, so that the remaining trains can run closer to time.

For passengers, the practical lesson is to check the running status of a train before leaving home. For the railways, the challenge is to make winter travel safe first and punctual second, in that order.

stimuli.title: Money that crosses borders
stimuli.content:
Every month, millions of Indians working abroad, in the Gulf, in Europe, in North America and elsewhere, send part of their earnings home. These transfers, known as remittances, have made India the largest recipient of such money in the world. For many families, the monthly transfer from a son or a husband abroad pays for food, school fees and medical bills, and over the years it has built houses, shops and small businesses.

Economists value remittances for reasons that go beyond the family budget. Unlike foreign investment, which may leave a country quickly when conditions turn bad, remittances tend to be steady, and they often rise when the home country faces a disaster, because workers abroad send more to help relatives in trouble. They also bring in foreign currency without creating any debt that must later be repaid.

The benefits, however, come with costs. Sending small sums across borders has long been expensive: once fees and the margin on the exchange rate are added, a worker may lose a noticeable share of what he sends. Many migrants also borrow heavily to pay recruitment agents before they leave, and spend their first years abroad simply clearing that debt. At home, families that depend on a single overseas earner are exposed if he loses his job or falls ill.

Some researchers worry about a subtler effect. Where remittances are large, they argue, young people may come to see migration as the only route to a good life, and invest little effort in local work or study. Others reply that the money often pays for the education that makes the next generation more productive.

Policy has focused on making transfers cheaper and safer. Digital channels have cut fees, and banks have been encouraged to offer accounts and investment products tailored to migrants and their families. The larger challenge is to turn money that is spent mainly on daily needs into savings and investment that can outlast the worker's years abroad.

stimuli.title: Pooling the milk
stimuli.content:
Twice a day, in thousands of Indian villages, a small queue forms outside a room with a tin roof. Farmers, many of them women, arrive carrying steel cans of milk from one or two buffaloes or cows. Each can is weighed, a small sample is tested for fat content, and within minutes the farmer receives a slip showing what she will be paid. This is the village collection centre of a dairy cooperative, and it is the first link in a chain that ends in packets of milk, butter and cheese on shop shelves hundreds of kilometres away.

Before cooperatives spread, a small producer had little choice but to sell to a private trader. With only a few litres to sell and no way of storing milk, which spoils within hours in the heat, she accepted whatever price the trader offered. Traders often paid late, cheated on measurement, or lent money on terms that tied the farmer to them for years.

The cooperative changed the balance of power by pooling the milk of many small producers. Together they could afford chilling plants, trucks and processing units, and could sell in distant cities where prices were higher. Because the members owned the organisation, its surplus returned to them, often as a bonus at the end of the year. Testing every sample also meant that the price depended on quality rather than on the trader's mood, so farmers had a reason to feed and care for their animals better.

The model is not free of problems. In some places, cooperatives have been captured by local politicians who use them to reward their supporters, and elections to their boards are bitterly fought. Private dairies, which now compete for the same milk, sometimes offer higher prices in good seasons, tempting members to sell outside.

Still, the basic idea has proved remarkably durable: when many small sellers act together, they can win terms that none of them could obtain alone.

stimuli.title: When winning means losing
stimuli.content:
Imagine a jar of coins put up for auction in a classroom. Nobody knows exactly how much money it contains, so each student makes a guess and bids accordingly. Some guesses are too low and some too high, and if the class is large, the average guess may be quite close to the true value. Yet the student who wins the auction is, almost by definition, the one whose guess was the most optimistic. Experiments of this kind repeatedly find that the winner pays more than the jar is worth.

Economists call this the winner's curse. It arises whenever many bidders compete for an item whose true value is the same for all of them but uncertain to each, such as the right to drill for oil in a particular field, a licence to use a band of radio frequencies, or a company that has been put up for sale. Every bidder's estimate contains some error. Winning therefore tells a bidder something unwelcome: that everyone else valued the prize less highly, and so her own estimate was probably too high.

The lesson for a careful bidder is counter-intuitive. Rather than bidding what she believes the item is worth, she should bid somewhat less, and shade her bid further as the number of rivals grows, because the more bidders there are, the more extreme the most optimistic estimate is likely to be. A bidder who ignores this may win often and still lose money.

The curse is not inevitable. Experienced bidders in industries with frequent auctions learn to discount their own enthusiasm, and the designers of an auction can reduce the problem by releasing more information about the item, which narrows the spread of estimates. Where bidders are inexperienced, or where pride and publicity reward winning for its own sake, the curse tends to bite hardest.

The idea reaches well beyond auctions. A company that wins a fierce bidding war to take over a rival, a city that outbids others to host a costly sporting event, even a buyer who beats a crowd of others to a house, may each discover that the victory was the most expensive part of the deal.

stimuli.title: When the totals mislead
stimuli.content:
A regional manager comparing two branches of a bank looks at a single figure: the share of loans repaid on time. The town branch recovers 88 per cent of its loans, the hill branch only 79 per cent. The conclusion seems obvious, and the hill branch is told to learn from its neighbour.

A closer look tells a different story. Each branch makes two kinds of loans: crop loans to small farmers, which are riskier because they depend on the weather, and salary loans to government employees, which are almost always repaid. Of the hill branch's 100 loans, 80 are crop loans, of which 60 were repaid, and 20 are salary loans, of which 19 were repaid. The town branch made only 20 crop loans, recovering 14, and 80 salary loans, recovering 74.

Now compare like with like. On crop loans, the hill branch recovers 75 per cent and the town branch 70 per cent. On salary loans, the hill branch recovers 95 per cent and the town branch 92.5 per cent. The hill branch does better in both categories, yet worse overall. It is not a weaker lender; it simply makes far more of the difficult loans.

This reversal is known as Simpson's paradox. It appears whenever the groups being compared differ in their mix of some factor that strongly affects the outcome. A hospital that treats the most serious cases can show a higher death rate than others even if it treats every type of patient better; a school that admits weaker students can post lower pass rates while adding more to each student's learning.

The paradox does not mean that totals are useless, nor that a breakdown always gives the truer picture. Splitting data by the wrong factor can create misleading patterns of its own. What it demands is a question before every comparison: are these groups really alike in the ways that matter? A manager who asked it might reward the hill branch for taking on the farmers whom others avoid, rather than scold it for the arithmetic that follows.

stimuli.title: The pot that keeps water cool
stimuli.content:
In many Indian homes, a round earthen pot still sits in a corner of the kitchen, (1) ______ with drinking water. Even on the hottest summer afternoon, the water inside stays pleasantly cool, although the pot uses no electricity at all and costs only a small sum at the local market.

The secret lies in the clay. Baked clay is full of tiny holes, so a little water slowly (2) ______ through the walls of the pot to its outer surface. There it evaporates, and evaporation carries heat away from the pot, just as sweat cools our skin on a hot day. The drier and (3) ______ the air, the faster the water evaporates and the cooler the pot becomes. In humid coastal weather, when the air is already full of moisture, the effect is much (4) ______.

Potters say that a new pot works best after it has been soaked and used for a few days. They also advise keeping it in a shady, airy place, and (5) ______ it regularly so that its tiny holes are not blocked by dust and by the salts left behind by the water.

In recent years, the earthen pot has found new admirers. Some families who own refrigerators still prefer it, because its water is cool without being icy and is gentler on the throat. Designers have used the same principle to build simple clay coolers for vegetables, which help small farmers and vendors keep their produce fresh for a few extra days. An old object, it seems, still has something to (6) ______ to a modern world that is worried about rising temperatures and electricity bills.

stimuli.title: The vanishing scavengers
stimuli.content:
Not long ago, vultures were a common sight in India, circling high above towns or crowding around the body of a dead cow at the edge of a village. Then, within roughly a decade from the 1990s, the numbers of several species (1) ______ by more than ninety per cent, one of the fastest declines of any bird ever recorded.

For years the cause remained a (2) ______. Scientists suspected disease or poisoning, but the answer turned out to be a common painkiller given to cattle. Vultures that fed on the bodies of animals treated shortly before death absorbed the drug, which (3) ______ their kidneys. Because a single carcass can feed dozens of birds, even a small share of treated animals was enough to kill vast numbers of them.

The loss was not only an ecological one. Vultures had quietly performed a public service, stripping a carcass to the bone within hours. Without them, carcasses lay rotting for days, and the number of stray dogs feeding on them rose. More dogs meant more dog bites and more cases of rabies, a disease that is almost always (4) ______ once its symptoms appear.

The veterinary use of the drug was banned, and breeding centres were set up to raise vultures in captivity and later release them into the wild. Progress has been slow, partly because vultures breed slowly, (5) ______ only one egg a year, and partly because some other painkillers that harm them remain in use.

The story is a reminder that the value of a species is not always obvious until it is gone. Animals that seem (6) ______, even unpleasant, may be holding up parts of the system on which human health depends.

stimuli.title: The trap of the minimum due
stimuli.content:
Every credit card statement shows two figures that matter: the total amount due, and a much smaller 'minimum amount due', usually a small percentage of the balance. Paying the minimum keeps the account in good standing and **(1) avoids** a late-payment fee. Many cardholders therefore treat it as the amount they owe. That is an expensive mistake.

Any part of the balance that is not paid by the due date begins to attract interest, often at rates of thirty to forty per cent a year, far **(2) lower** than the rate on almost any other kind of borrowing. Worse, on many cards the interest-free period on new purchases is lost as long as an old balance is carried forward, so even fresh spending starts attracting interest from the day it is made. A cardholder who pays only the minimum each month may find, after a year of steady payments, that the balance has barely **(3) fallen**.

The design is not accidental. Card issuers earn much of their income from customers who **(4) clear** their balances from month to month, and a low minimum makes this easy to do. In the United States, for example, card statements must show how long it would take to repay the balance through minimum payments alone, and how much would be paid in total along the way; the figures are often **(5) sobering**.

The remedy is simple to state, if not always to follow: treat the card as a convenient way to pay, not as a source of credit, and settle the full amount every month. A cardholder who cannot do so is, in effect, borrowing at one of the highest rates on offer, and would usually be better off **(6) increasing** the card balance with a cheaper personal loan.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, who are most of the presenters at the station described in the first paragraph?

options.text: Owners of the shops in the town market
Local people who had never used a microphone before
Trained broadcasters hired from the nearest city
Agriculture officers posted in the district

solution.concept: Locating a stated detail
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'most of its presenters are farmers, housewives and students who had never spoken into a microphone before'.
steps: They had never spoken into a microphone
solution.why_others_wrong: Trained broadcasters from a city are the opposite of what is described. An agriculture officer gives one talk in paragraph 2 but is not a regular presenter. The station sits above a grocery shop, but shop owners are not named as presenters.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Local people who had never used a microphone before

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: How, according to the passage, does a community station differ from a large commercial channel?

options.text: It plays only music and carries no talk shows.
It broadcasts across a whole state in one language.
It is run by the government and needs no licence.
It serves a few villages and uses their own dialect.

solution.concept: Locating a stated contrast
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: commercial channels try to reach as many listeners as possible across a city or state, while 'a community station serves a few villages and speaks in their own dialect'.
steps: Find 'Unlike large commercial channels' in paragraph 2
Commercial: as many listeners as possible
Community: a few villages, their own dialect
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 2 lists talks and call-in shows, so 'only music' is wrong. Broadcasting across a state describes the commercial channels. Paragraph 4 says stations are run by schools, colleges and voluntary groups and that licences take time to obtain.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It serves a few villages and uses their own dialect.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, have community stations been especially useful during floods and storms?

options.text: They sent their volunteers to rescue stranded families.
They raised money to rebuild houses after the floods.
They kept villages informed when mobile networks failed.
They moved their studios to the relief camps.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'During floods and heavy storms, when mobile networks often fail, community stations have kept villages informed about rising water levels, safe shelters and relief camps.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Raising money, rescuing families and moving studios are never mentioned. The passage says the stations gave information, not that they did relief work.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They kept villages informed when mobile networks failed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a difficulty in running a community station?

options.text: Most stations have very little money.
Programmes in local dialects are not permitted.
Only a limited amount of advertising is allowed.
Trained volunteers move away to cities.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists little money, limited advertising, equipment that breaks down, volunteers who move away and slow licences. Far from being forbidden, local dialects are a feature of these stations (paragraph 2).
solution.why_others_wrong: Little money, volunteers leaving and the limit on advertising are all stated in paragraph 4, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Programmes in local dialects are not permitted.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'shaped' as used in the passage ('Its programmes are shaped by local needs')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: shaped by = formed or decided by
solution.explanation: The next sentence lists programmes chosen for local people: pest control, a pension scheme, local songs and market prices. Local needs decide what is broadcast, so 'shaped' means influenced or determined.
steps: Context: the programmes listed all answer local needs
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Shortened', 'hidden' and 'repeated' say nothing about local needs deciding what goes on air.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How to Become a Radio Star

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: Every paragraph is about small stations run by and for local people: what they are, what they broadcast, why villagers trust them, their difficulties and how listeners keep them going.
steps: Paras 1-2: local stations for local people
Para 5: the station belongs to its listeners
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage does not say radio is declining. Becoming a star is never discussed. Advertising appears in a single sentence as one difficulty, so it is too narrow for a title.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A Voice for the Village

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what is the main reason why trains run late in thick fog?

options.text: Railway staff are on leave during the winter season.
Drivers cannot see signals, so trains must slow down.
Passengers take longer to board in the cold weather.
Fog damages the electric lines that run the trains.

solution.concept: Locating a stated cause
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'A driver who cannot see the signal ahead cannot safely run his train at full speed.' Paragraph 2 adds that rules require trains to slow down sharply in thick fog.
steps: Driver cannot see the signal ahead
solution.why_others_wrong: Damaged lines, slow boarding and staff on leave are never mentioned. The passage also rejects 'poor planning' as the main cause.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Drivers cannot see signals, so trains must slow down.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, is it dangerous for a driver to spot a red signal late?

options.text: A heavy train needs a long distance to stop after braking.
Other drivers cannot see his train's headlights.
The signal may change back to green at any moment.
The brakes of most trains do not work in cold weather.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: a driver 'may not spot a red signal until it is too late. A heavy train needs a long distance to halt even after the brakes are applied.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Signals changing back, headlights and brakes failing in the cold are never mentioned in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A heavy train needs a long distance to stop after braking.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'eased' as used in the passage ('Technology has eased the problem without removing it')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: ease a problem = make it less severe
solution.explanation: The words 'without removing it' show that the problem still exists but is smaller. To ease a problem is to make it less serious: to reduce it.
steps: The problem remains but is smaller
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Solved' contradicts 'without removing it'. 'Created' is the opposite of what the device does. 'Hidden' does not describe making a problem smaller.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why do railways cancel or shorten some services in the foggiest weeks?

options.text: Satellite devices cannot be fitted to all the locomotives in time for winter.
Shorter routes are cheaper to run when ticket sales fall in bad weather.
Passengers do not wish to travel during the coldest weeks of the winter.
Running fewer trains means delays spread less, so the rest run closer to time.

solution.concept: Inference: linking a stated action to the cause given just before it
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that one late train holds up the trains behind it and the effect spreads. Running fewer trains reduces this knock-on effect, 'so that the remaining trains can run closer to time'.
steps: Problem: one late train delays those behind it
Purpose stated: remaining trains run closer to time
solution.why_others_wrong: Passengers' wishes, a shortage of devices and falling ticket sales are not given as reasons; the passage links the cuts only to the spread of delays.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Running fewer trains means delays spread less, so the rest run closer to time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the last sentence of the passage ('safe first and punctual second, in that order') imply?

options.text: Safety devices have already made fog delays a thing of the past.
Delays are acceptable if they are needed to keep trains safe.
Punctuality matters more to passengers than safety does.
Trains should be cancelled whenever there is any fog.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of an order of priorities
solution.explanation: Putting safety first and punctuality second 'in that order' means that when the two clash, safety wins: trains may run late so that they run safely.
steps: So some delay is acceptable for safety
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Punctuality matters more' reverses the order. Cancelling trains whenever there is any fog goes far beyond the passage. Paragraph 4 says delays cannot be avoided entirely, so they are not a thing of the past.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Delays are acceptable if they are needed to keep trains safe.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?

solution.concept: Tone: how the author treats the subject
solution.explanation: The author explains how signals work, why fog slows trains and what technology does, and ends with practical advice for passengers. The writing is calm and informative.
solution.why_others_wrong: The author defends the railways against the charge of poor planning, so the tone is not accusing. There are no jokes. Describing devices that remove much of the guesswork is not hopeless.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, are remittances considered more dependable than foreign investment?

options.text: They are guaranteed by the governments of the countries that send them.
They are steady and often rise when the home country faces a disaster.
They are sent through banks, which cannot move money out of the country.
They are always spent on houses and businesses rather than daily needs.

solution.concept: Locating a stated contrast
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: foreign investment 'may leave a country quickly when conditions turn bad', whereas remittances 'tend to be steady, and they often rise when the home country faces a disaster'.
steps: Remittances: steady, often rise in a disaster
solution.why_others_wrong: No guarantee by foreign governments is mentioned. The last paragraph says remittances are spent mainly on daily needs, which contradicts 'always spent on houses'. Banks being unable to move money is never stated.
solution.final_answer: Option B: They are steady and often rise when the home country faces a disaster.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a cost or risk linked to remittances?

options.text: Families depending on a single overseas earner
Debts taken to pay recruitment agents before leaving
A stronger rupee that hurts the country's exporters
Fees and exchange-rate margins on small transfers

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists fees and exchange margins, debts to recruitment agents and the exposure of families relying on one earner. The effect of remittances on the rupee or on exporters is never discussed.
steps: Stronger rupee and exporters: not in the passage
solution.why_others_wrong: Fees, recruitment debts and dependence on one earner are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A stronger rupee that hurts the country's exporters

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the phrase 'without creating any debt that must later be repaid' suggest about some other sources of foreign currency?

options.text: They are always smaller than the money migrants send.
They are spent only by the government, not by families.
They are not allowed to enter the country at all.
They come as loans that the country must pay back.

solution.concept: Inference: what a contrast implies about the thing it is contrasted with
solution.explanation: Praising remittances for bringing in foreign currency 'without creating any debt' implies that other ways of getting foreign currency, such as borrowing abroad, do create debt that must be repaid.
steps: The contrast implies others bring debt
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing suggests other sources are banned, always smaller, or used only by the government; the phrase is about debt, not size or who spends the money.
solution.final_answer: Option D: They come as loans that the country must pay back.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: On which point do the researchers mentioned in paragraph 4 disagree?

options.text: Whether remittances discourage effort or fund a more productive next generation
Whether young people should study abroad or in their home towns
Whether migrants should pay recruitment agents before they leave the country
Whether digital channels have really cut the fees charged on transfers

solution.concept: Inference: identifying the issue in a two-sided debate
solution.explanation: One group argues that large remittances may lead young people to invest little effort in local work or study; the other replies that the money often pays for education that makes the next generation more productive. The dispute is about the effect of remittances on young people's effort and productivity.
steps: View 1: remittances weaken effort at home
Issue: effect on the next generation's productivity
solution.why_others_wrong: Recruitment agents and digital fees appear in other paragraphs and are not debated. Studying abroad versus at home is not what either side discusses.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Whether remittances discourage effort or fund a more productive next generation

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'tailored' as used in the passage ('accounts and investment products tailored to migrants and their families')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: tailored to = made to fit particular needs
solution.explanation: Banks are encouraged to offer products made for the particular needs of migrants. Like clothes cut to fit one person, the products are designed to suit them.
steps: Context: banks offering products for a group
Made to fit that group's needs
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Stitched' is the literal tailor's sense and does not apply to accounts. 'Sold cheaply' and 'restricted' are not meanings of 'tailored'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Digital channels have solved every problem linked to sending money home.
Recruitment agents are the main reason why Indians go abroad to work.
Remittances do more harm than good and should be discouraged.
Remittances help families and the economy but carry costs and need better use.

solution.concept: Main idea: balance the benefits, the costs and the conclusion
solution.explanation: The passage describes the benefits (family income, steady foreign currency), the costs (fees, debts, dependence), a debate, and ends by calling for cheaper transfers and for turning the money into lasting savings.
steps: Para 5: cheaper transfers, better use of the money
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage never calls for remittances to be discouraged. Recruitment agents are one cost among several. The last paragraph says a 'larger challenge' remains, so not every problem is solved.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Remittances help families and the economy but carry costs and need better use.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, did small producers accept whatever price a private trader offered?

options.text: The government fixed the price that traders had to pay.
Traders always paid in advance for a whole year's milk.
They had little milk to sell and no way to stop it spoiling.
They preferred traders to the cooperative's testing system.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'With only a few litres to sell and no way of storing milk, which spoils within hours in the heat, she accepted whatever price the trader offered.'
solution.why_others_wrong: A government-fixed price is never mentioned. Traders 'often paid late', the opposite of paying in advance. The cooperative did not yet exist in the period described, so farmers could not prefer traders to it.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They had little milk to sell and no way to stop it spoiling.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how did testing every sample of milk benefit farmers?

options.text: It let them keep their milk fresh for several days longer.
It allowed them to sell their milk without weighing it.
It made the price depend on quality, rewarding better care of animals.
It removed the need for chilling plants and trucks.

solution.concept: Locating a stated effect
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: testing 'meant that the price depended on quality rather than on the trader's mood, so farmers had a reason to feed and care for their animals better'.
steps: Reason to care for animals better
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 1 says each can is weighed as well as tested. Testing does not keep milk fresh. Chilling plants and trucks are listed as things the pooled cooperative could afford, not things testing replaced.
solution.final_answer: Option C: It made the price depend on quality, rewarding better care of animals.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The statement that the cooperative 'changed the balance of power' implies that earlier

options.text: traders had the stronger hand in dealing with farmers
the government controlled the sale of all milk
farmers refused to sell milk to anyone outside the village
farmers and traders bargained as equals

solution.concept: Inference: what a change implies about the situation before it
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows traders setting prices, paying late, cheating on measurement and tying farmers to them with loans. If the cooperative changed the balance of power, power earlier lay with the traders.
steps: Para 2: traders set prices, cheated, tied farmers down
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Bargained as equals' contradicts paragraph 2. Government control and a refusal to sell outside the village are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option A: traders had the stronger hand in dealing with farmers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the passage suggest about why elections to cooperative boards are 'bitterly fought'?

options.text: Control of a cooperative can bring power to reward supporters.
Only women are allowed to vote in the elections.
Board members must pay for the chilling plants themselves.
Private dairies choose the members of the boards.

solution.concept: Inference: connecting two parts of the same sentence
solution.explanation: The same sentence says cooperatives have been 'captured by local politicians who use them to reward their supporters'. A board that can hand out favours is a prize worth fighting for.
steps: They use them to reward supporters
So board seats are worth fighting for
solution.why_others_wrong: Paying for plants, private dairies choosing boards and women-only voting are not in the passage; the passage links the fights only to political capture.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Control of a cooperative can bring power to reward supporters.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'captured' as used in the passage ('cooperatives have been captured by local politicians')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: capture (an organisation) = take control of it for one's own purposes
solution.explanation: The politicians 'use them to reward their supporters', which shows that they control the cooperatives. To capture an organisation here is to take control of it.
steps: Context: politicians use cooperatives to reward supporters
They have gained control of them
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Arrested' and 'photographed' are literal senses of 'capture' that cannot apply to an organisation. 'Won in a battle' suggests fighting with weapons, while the passage describes political control.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How to Test Milk for Fat

solution.concept: Title: the central idea, stated in the last paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage ends: 'when many small sellers act together, they can win terms that none of them could obtain alone.' Small producers gaining strength by joining together is captured by 'Strength in Numbers'.
steps: Para 3: pooling gives small producers power
Para 5: acting together wins better terms
solution.why_others_wrong: Testing milk is one detail. Private dairies paying more is mentioned once, and only in good seasons. The trader appears only in paragraph 2 as the problem the cooperative solved.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the reasoning of the passage, is winning an auction 'unwelcome' news for a bidder?

options.text: It proves that her rivals deliberately bid low to trick her.
It shows that the seller has hidden important facts about the item.
It reveals that all the rivals valued the item lower than she did.
It means she must now pay fees to the people who organised the sale.

solution.concept: Inference: following the author's chain of reasoning
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: winning tells a bidder 'that everyone else valued the prize less highly, and so her own estimate was probably too high'. Since all estimates contain error, being the highest suggests hers had the biggest upward error.
steps: So her estimate was probably too high
solution.why_others_wrong: Hidden facts, organisers' fees and deliberate tricks by rivals are not part of the argument; the curse arises even when everyone bids honestly on the same uncertain value.
solution.final_answer: Option C: It reveals that all the rivals valued the item lower than she did.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how should a careful bidder change her bid as the number of rival bidders increases?

options.text: Lower it further, because the top estimate grows more extreme.
Raise it, because more rivals mean she is less likely to win.
Withdraw from the auction once there are more than a few rivals.
Keep it fixed at her best guess of what the item is worth.

solution.concept: Inference: applying the stated rule and its reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: she should 'shade her bid further as the number of rivals grows, because the more bidders there are, the more extreme the most optimistic estimate is likely to be'.
steps: More bidders → more extreme highest estimate
Winning then signals a bigger overestimate
solution.why_others_wrong: Raising the bid is the instinct the passage warns against. Bidding her best guess is what the passage says she should not do ('Rather than bidding what she believes the item is worth'). Withdrawing is never advised.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Lower it further, because the top estimate grows more extreme.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following situations is the winner's curse, as defined in the passage, LEAST likely to arise?

options.text: Telecom firms bidding for a licence to use a band of frequencies
Investors bidding for a company whose future profits are uncertain
A collector bidding for a painting she wants for her own home
Oil companies bidding for the right to drill in an unexplored field

solution.concept: Inference: applying a definition to new cases
solution.explanation: The curse needs an item whose value is the same for all bidders but uncertain to each. A painting bought for one's own wall is worth different amounts to different people, and the collector knows what it is worth to her, so winning does not reveal that she overestimated a common value.
steps: Condition 1: value the same for all bidders
Condition 2: that value uncertain to each
solution.why_others_wrong: The oil field, the frequency licence and the company are the passage's own examples of a common but uncertain value, so the curse is likely in each of them.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A collector bidding for a painting she wants for her own home

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, does releasing more information about an item reduce the winner's curse?

options.text: It persuades inexperienced bidders to stay away from the auction.
It makes pride and publicity less important to the bidders.
It allows the seller to set a higher minimum price for the item.
It narrows the spread of estimates, so the highest is nearer the truth.

solution.concept: Inference: explaining why a remedy works
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says more information 'narrows the spread of estimates'. If estimates are bunched closer together, the most optimistic one is not far above the true value, so the winner overpays by less.
solution.why_others_wrong: Keeping bidders away, raising the minimum price and reducing pride are not effects the passage attributes to more information.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It narrows the spread of estimates, so the highest is nearer the truth.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'shade' as used in the passage ('shade her bid further as the number of rivals grows')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: shade (a figure) = adjust it slightly, here downwards
solution.explanation: The sentence tells the bidder to bid 'somewhat less' than her estimate, and to do so 'further' when there are more rivals. To shade a bid here is to lower it a little.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hide from view', 'keep it safe' and 'make darker' are other senses of 'shade' that do not fit a number being adjusted.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's approach in the passage?

options.text: Sarcastic, mocking companies that lose money in takeover battles
Analytical, explaining a counter-intuitive risk and how to guard against it
Alarmist, demanding that governments stop selling licences by auction
Nostalgic, recalling a classroom game that the author once enjoyed

solution.concept: Tone: identify the purpose and manner of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The author uses an experiment to explain a concept, gives its conditions and a remedy, and applies it to other situations. This is a calm, analytical explanation of a counter-intuitive risk.
steps: Example → concept → advice → remedies → wider uses
solution.why_others_wrong: The classroom jar is a thought experiment, not a memory. Takeovers are mentioned without mockery. The author says the curse 'is not inevitable' and never calls for auctions to be stopped.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Analytical, explaining a counter-intuitive risk and how to guard against it

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, does the hill branch's overall recovery rate look worse than the town branch's?

options.text: It recovers a smaller share of both crop loans and salary loans.
Most of its loans are crop loans, which are repaid less often.
It made far fewer loans in total than the town branch did.
Its salary loans go to employees who are rarely paid on time.

solution.concept: Inference: explaining a reversal by the mix of groups
solution.explanation: Both branches made 100 loans. The hill branch does better in each category (75% vs 70%, 95% vs 92.5%), but 80 of its 100 loans are risky crop loans, against only 20 at the town branch. Given the town branch's mix, its own rates would give 91%, above the town branch's 88%.
steps: Hill is better in each category
Hill's mix: 80 crop loans vs town's 20
The mix, not skill, drags its total down
solution.why_others_wrong: The hill branch recovers a larger share in both categories, not a smaller one. Both branches made 100 loans. Salary loans are described as 'almost always repaid', and the hill branch recovers 19 of 20.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Most of its loans are crop loans, which are repaid less often.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Suppose the town branch made 20 more crop loans and recovered 14 of them, with its salary loans unchanged. What would its overall recovery rate then be?

solution.concept: Inference: recomputing an overall rate after the mix changes
solution.explanation: Crop loans become 20 + 20 = 40, with 14 + 14 = 28 repaid; salary loans stay at 80 with 74 repaid. Overall: (28 + 74) ÷ (40 + 80) = 102 ÷ 120 = 85 per cent. Adding more risky loans pulls the total down even though the crop-loan rate (70%) is unchanged.
solution.shortcut: Overall rate = total repaid ÷ total loans = (28 + 74) ÷ 120 = 85%
solution.why_others_wrong: 88 per cent ignores the new loans. About 81 per cent is the simple average of the two category rates ((70 + 92.5) ÷ 2 = 81.25), which ignores how many loans fall in each. About 73 per cent counts the 20 new loans but forgets the 14 that were repaid ((14 + 74) ÷ 120).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The example of the hospital in paragraph 4 is used to show that

options.text: patients should always choose the hospital with the lowest death rate
hospitals should refuse the most serious cases to protect their records
a raw comparison can make those who take the hardest cases look worse
death rates are a poor measure of a hospital's work in every situation

solution.concept: Inference: the purpose of an example
solution.explanation: Like the hill branch, a hospital that takes the most serious cases can do better with every type of patient yet show a worse overall figure. The example shows that raw totals can penalise those who take on the hardest cases.
steps: Hill branch: hardest loans, worse total
Same lesson: raw totals can mislead
solution.why_others_wrong: The author does not recommend refusing serious cases; the last line praises taking on hard cases. Paragraph 5 says totals are not useless, so 'in every situation' goes too far. Choosing the lowest death rate is exactly the mistake the example warns against.
solution.final_answer: Option C: a raw comparison can make those who take the hardest cases look worse

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by saying that 'Splitting data by the wrong factor can create misleading patterns of its own'?

options.text: Every comparison of branches should be split into as many groups as possible.
A breakdown is useful only if it is by a factor that really affects the outcome.
Simpson's paradox appears only when data are split into exactly two groups.
Totals should never be broken down, because breakdowns always mislead.

solution.concept: Inference: reading a qualification of the main argument
solution.explanation: The author warns against treating any breakdown as automatically truer. The useful question is whether the groups differ 'in the ways that matter', so a breakdown helps only when it is by a factor that genuinely affects the result.
steps: The wrong factor can mislead too
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Never be broken down' contradicts the whole branch example. 'As many groups as possible' ignores the warning about the wrong factor. The number of groups is not the author's point.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A breakdown is useful only if it is by a factor that really affects the outcome.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'post' as used in the passage ('a school that admits weaker students can post lower pass rates')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: post (results, figures) = record or report them
solution.explanation: A school does not mail or appoint its pass rates; it records and reports them. 'Post lower pass rates' means show lower pass rates in its results.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Mail', 'appoint' and 'display on a wall' are other senses of 'post' that do not fit figures a school achieves.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best expresses the central lesson of the passage?

options.text: Compare groups only after checking that they are alike in what matters.
Branches that lend to farmers should be closed to protect the bank.
Hospitals and schools should be judged by the same rules as banks.
Overall figures are always more reliable than detailed breakdowns.

solution.concept: Main idea: the question the author says every comparison demands
solution.explanation: The passage ends with the question that the paradox demands: 'are these groups really alike in the ways that matter?' Its lesson is to check that groups are alike before comparing their totals.
steps: Last paragraph: ask whether the groups are alike
solution.why_others_wrong: The author praises lending to farmers. The passage shows how totals can mislead, so they are not 'always more reliable'. Hospitals and schools are examples, not the subject of a recommendation.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Compare groups only after checking that they are alike in what matters.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'with drinking water' needs a word meaning 'containing'
solution.explanation: The pot holds drinking water that 'stays pleasantly cool', so it is filled with water.
steps: The next sentence: the water inside stays cool
solution.why_others_wrong: A pot 'emptied with water' or 'broken with water' makes no sense, and an emptied or broken pot could not keep water cool. 'Painted with drinking water' is meaningless.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: slow movement of water through tiny holes
solution.explanation: Water that passes slowly, a little at a time, through the tiny holes in clay 'trickles' through the walls.
steps: Slow movement of a small amount of liquid
solution.why_others_wrong: Water does not 'leap' or 'burn' through clay. 'Freezes' contradicts the hot weather and the evaporation in the next sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: conditions that speed up evaporation
solution.explanation: Water evaporates faster in dry, warm air. The sentence pairs 'drier' with a second quality that helps evaporation: 'warmer'. It also fits the opening point that the pot works on the hottest afternoons.
steps: Evaporation is faster in warm air
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Wetter' contradicts 'drier' and the next sentence, which says humid air weakens the effect. Colder air slows evaporation. 'Darker' has nothing to do with evaporation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: humid air slows evaporation, so the cooling is less
solution.explanation: Air 'already full of moisture' takes up water slowly, so less evaporation happens and the pot cools less. The effect is much weaker.
steps: Clue: air already full of moisture
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Stronger' and 'faster' reverse the effect of humid air described in the passage. 'Louder' does not describe cooling.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the purpose clause after the blank decides the word
solution.explanation: The pot must be treated 'so that its tiny holes are not blocked by dust and ... salts'. Removing dust and salts means cleaning it regularly.
steps: Purpose: keep the holes free of dust and salts
solution.why_others_wrong: Painting or covering the pot would block its holes, the opposite of the purpose. Heating it does not remove dust or salts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'have something to ___ to someone' = have something useful to give
solution.explanation: An old object that saves electricity and keeps things cool can offer a lesson to a world worried about heat and power bills: it still has something to offer to it.
steps: Structure: 'something to ___ to a modern world'
The pot has something useful to give
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fear to a modern world' and 'hide to a modern world' are ungrammatical. 'Something to refuse to a modern world' contradicts the praise of the pot in the paragraph.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'one of the fastest declines' decides the direction
solution.explanation: The sentence ends by calling this 'one of the fastest declines of any bird', so the numbers fell by more than ninety per cent.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rose' and 'doubled' are increases, which contradict 'declines'. 'Settled by more than ninety per cent' is meaningless.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'For years' and 'Scientists suspected' show the cause was unknown
solution.explanation: Scientists only 'suspected' causes until 'the answer turned out to be' a painkiller. Something unexplained for years is a mystery.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Certainty' contradicts the guessing that followed. 'Celebration' and 'decision' do not describe an unknown cause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the drug killed the birds, so it harmed an organ
solution.explanation: The next sentence says the drug was 'enough to kill vast numbers' of vultures. A drug that kills by acting on the kidneys damaged them.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cleaned', 'strengthened' and 'cooled' describe harmless or helpful effects, which cannot explain mass deaths.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the word must make rabies a reason for concern
solution.explanation: The paragraph lists harms that followed the loss of vultures. Rabies is a serious harm because, once symptoms appear, it almost always kills: it is fatal.
steps: Context: harms caused by more dogs
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Curable' and 'mild' would make rabies a small matter, which does not fit a list of serious harms. 'Rare' contradicts 'more cases of rabies'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the participle phrase explains 'breed slowly'
solution.explanation: Vultures breed slowly because each pair produces only one egg a year, that is, they lay only one egg a year.
steps: Explanation: only one egg a year
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Eating', 'hiding' and 'selling' one egg a year do not explain slow breeding, and birds do not sell eggs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'seem ___, even unpleasant' is contrasted with real value
solution.explanation: The passage says a species' value 'is not always obvious'. Animals that seem of no value, even unpleasant, may in fact be important: they seem worthless.
steps: 'seem ___, even unpleasant' → seem to have no value
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Precious' and 'beautiful' would mean the value is already obvious, and do not build up to 'even unpleasant'. 'Endangered' is about numbers, not about how valuable an animal seems.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'Paying the minimum keeps the account in good standing and avoids a late-payment fee'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the 'and' clause must state a benefit, like 'good standing'
solution.explanation: Paying at least the minimum keeps the account in good standing and so escapes the fee charged for late payment. 'Avoids' is correct; it also explains why many people think the minimum is enough.
steps: First benefit: account in good standing
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Incurs' (brings on) and 'doubles' turn the benefit into a penalty. 'Waives' is what a bank does, not what a payment does.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'often at rates of thirty to forty per cent a year, far lower than the rate on almost any other kind of borrowing'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: thirty to forty per cent a year is a very high rate
solution.explanation: Rates of thirty to forty per cent are far above those on home, car or personal loans. The last paragraph ('one of the highest rates on offer') confirms that card interest is far higher, not lower.
steps: Last paragraph: 'one of the highest rates on offer'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Safer' and 'fairer' do not compare the cost of borrowing. 'Lower' contradicts the figures and the last paragraph, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'may find, after a year of steady payments, that the balance has barely fallen'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the surprise is that steady payments hardly reduce the balance
solution.explanation: Because most of each minimum payment goes on interest, a year of steady payments reduces the balance only a little: it has 'barely fallen'. 'Fallen' is correct.
steps: Steady payments → one expects the balance to fall
High interest eats most of each payment
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Barely doubled' and 'barely vanished' are contradictory phrases. 'Barely risen' implies the balance was expected to rise, which makes no sense after a year of payments.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'Card issuers earn much of their income from customers who clear their balances from month to month, and a low minimum makes this easy to do'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: issuers earn interest only on unpaid balances
solution.explanation: Interest is charged on balances that are not paid off. Issuers earn from customers who roll over (carry forward) their balances from month to month, and a low minimum makes this easy. Customers who clear their balances pay no interest.
steps: A low minimum lets people leave balances unpaid
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Check their balances' does not produce interest income. 'Close their balances from month to month' is meaningless. 'Clear' reverses the logic, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'how long it would take to repay the balance through minimum payments alone, and how much would be paid in total along the way; the figures are often sobering'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the figures reveal a long, costly repayment
solution.explanation: Repaying through minimum payments alone takes years and costs far more than the original balance. Figures that make people think seriously about a danger are 'sobering'. The word is correct.
steps: Minimum payments → very long, very costly repayment
Such figures shock people into caution
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Reassuring', 'trivial' and 'cheerful' contradict the passage's warning that paying only the minimum is 'an expensive mistake'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (6) may be wrongly used: 'would usually be better off increasing the card balance with a cheaper personal loan'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: a cheaper loan should take the place of the costly card debt
solution.explanation: A cardholder paying one of the highest rates would be better off paying off the card with a cheaper loan: replacing the card balance with a personal loan. 'Increasing' the costly balance makes no sense.
steps: A cheaper loan can pay it off
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ignoring' and 'doubling' the card balance would make matters worse. 'Increasing' contradicts 'better off', so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
My elder brother he (A) / works as a clerk (B) / in a cooperative bank. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: A clause has one subject; a pronoun does not repeat a noun subject that has just been named
solution.explanation: 'My elder brother' is already the subject of 'works'. Adding 'he' gives the verb two subjects. Correct: 'My elder brother works as a clerk in a cooperative bank.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B has a singular verb that agrees with 'brother'. Part C is a correct place phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: My elder brother he

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
All the members of the society (A) / are agree with (B) / the new timings of the branch. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: All the members of the society
the new timings of the branch.

solution.concept: 'Agree' is a verb, not an adjective, so it is not used after 'am/is/are'
solution.explanation: 'Agree' is a full verb: 'All the members agree with the new timings'. 'Are agree' wrongly adds the verb 'be' before it, as if 'agree' were an adjective like 'happy'.
steps: A verb does not need 'are' before it
'are agree with' → 'agree with': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct plural subject. Part C is a correct object phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
One or two customers (A) / has complained about (B) / the noise from the new generator. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the noise from the new generator.

solution.concept: 'One or two' + plural noun takes a plural verb (unlike 'more than one' + singular noun)
solution.explanation: 'One or two customers' means a few customers; the noun is plural and so is the verb: 'One or two customers have complained about the noise ...'.
steps: 'has complained' → 'have complained': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses the plural noun 'customers' after 'one or two'. Part C is a correct object phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Fifty new staffs (A) / have been recruited (B) / for the bank's rural branches. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Staff' (the people who work for an organisation) is a collective noun with no '-s' plural in this sense
solution.explanation: 'Staff' already refers to a group of employees, so it does not take '-s' when counting people: 'Fifty new staff (or staff members) have been recruited ...'.
steps: 'Fifty new staffs' → 'Fifty new staff members': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B's plural verb suits a subject of fifty people. Part C is a correct prepositional phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The cashier absented (A) / from the office for two days (B) / without informing the manager. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: from the office for two days

solution.concept: 'Absent' as a verb is reflexive: absent oneself (from a place)
solution.explanation: The verb 'absent' needs a reflexive pronoun: 'The cashier absented himself from the office for two days ...'. Without 'himself', the verb has no object.
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B correctly uses 'from' for the place and 'for' for the period. Part C is a correct gerund phrase after 'without'. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
