Every member of the society (A) / must abide to (B) / the rules framed by its board. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: the rules framed by its board.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: abide by (a rule, decision or agreement) = obey it
solution.explanation: The phrasal verb meaning 'obey' is 'abide by': 'Every member of the society must abide by the rules framed by its board.'
steps: 'abide to' → 'abide by': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct singular subject. Part C is a correct object with a participle phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new software (A) / is capable to handle (B) / ten thousand transactions a minute. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Capable' takes 'of' + -ing (capable of doing), not a to-infinitive
solution.explanation: The adjective 'capable' is followed by 'of' and a gerund: 'The new software is capable of handling ten thousand transactions a minute.' (Compare 'able to handle'.)
steps: 'capable to handle' → 'capable of handling': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject. Part C is a correct object with a rate ('a minute'). B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: is capable to handle

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
All applicants must submit (A) / the signed forms (B) / till the fifteenth of this month. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: till the fifteenth of this month.

solution.concept: 'By' marks a deadline (no later than); 'till/until' marks how long a situation continues
solution.explanation: Submitting a form is a single action that must happen no later than a date, so the preposition is 'by': '... must submit the signed forms by the fifteenth of this month.' 'Till' would suggest that applicants keep submitting until that date.
steps: 'till the fifteenth' → 'by the fifteenth': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'must' + base verb. Part B is a correct object. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: till the fifteenth of this month.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The power supply to the branch (A) / was cut off (B) / during three hours this morning. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The power supply to the branch

solution.concept: 'For' + a length of time (for three hours); 'during' + a named period or event (during the night, during the meeting)
solution.explanation: 'Three hours' measures how long the cut lasted, which needs 'for': 'was cut off for three hours this morning'. 'During' is used with a period named as a whole, such as 'during the morning'.
steps: 'during three hours' → 'for three hours': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject. Part B is a correct passive of the phrasal verb 'cut off'. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: during three hours this morning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Having been warned twice by the auditors, (A) / the clerk now checks every voucher (B) / before filing it. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Having been warned twice by the auditors,
the clerk now checks every voucher

solution.concept: Perfect passive participle ('Having been + past participle') whose subject is the subject of the main clause
solution.explanation: The clerk was warned (passive) before he began checking. 'Having been warned twice by the auditors' correctly refers to 'the clerk', the subject of the main clause. 'Before filing it' correctly uses a gerund after the preposition 'before'.
steps: Part A: perfect passive participle, doer of 'warned' = auditors: correct
Part B: its subject 'the clerk' is the one who was warned: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. The participle does not dangle, because the clerk is the one who was warned.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
When I met him in 2020, (A) / he told me that he had left (B) / the bank three years ago. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: he told me that he had left

solution.concept: 'Ago' counts back from now; to count back from a past point, use 'before' or 'earlier'
solution.explanation: He left the bank three years before 2020, not three years before today. Seen from a past moment, the right word is 'before' or 'earlier': '... he had left the bank three years before (or earlier).'
steps: 'three years ago' → 'three years before': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct past time clause. Part B correctly uses the past perfect for the earlier action. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: the bank three years ago.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Many first-time borrowers are unsure (A) / if to choose a fixed rate (B) / or a floating one. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: if to choose a fixed rate

solution.concept: Before a to-infinitive, only 'whether' can introduce the choice ('whether to'); 'if to' is never used
solution.explanation: A yes/no or either/or choice followed by an infinitive must begin with 'whether': 'Many first-time borrowers are unsure whether to choose a fixed rate or a floating one.' 'If' can introduce a full clause ('unsure if they should choose ...') but never a bare to-infinitive.
steps: Choice expressed with a to-infinitive: '___ to choose'
'if to choose' → 'whether to choose': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and adjective. Part C correctly completes the choice with 'or a floating one'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: if to choose a fixed rate

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The officer said that if the documents were in order (A) / that the loan would be released (B) / within a week of the visit. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The officer said that if the documents were in order
that the loan would be released
within a week of the visit.

solution.concept: A reported clause takes one 'that'; it is not repeated after an inserted 'if' clause
solution.explanation: 'Said that' already introduces the reported clause. The 'if' clause is inserted inside it, so the main part continues without a second 'that': 'The officer said that if the documents were in order, the loan would be released within a week of the visit.'
steps: 'if the documents were in order' is inserted inside it
The second 'that' repeats the first: error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly backshifts to 'were' after 'said'. Part C is a correct time phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: that the loan would be released

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
After three attempts, the shopkeeper finally **succeeded to get** a loan for his new shop.

solution.concept: 'Succeed' takes 'in' + -ing (succeed in doing something)
solution.explanation: The verb 'succeed' is followed by 'in' and a gerund: 'the shopkeeper finally succeeded in getting a loan'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Succeeded for getting' uses the wrong preposition. 'Succeeded getting' leaves out the preposition. The original uses a to-infinitive, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Do you **know to operate** the new cash-counting machine?

solution.concept: 'Know' + a question word + to-infinitive (know how to do something), not 'know' + to-infinitive
solution.explanation: To talk about having a skill, English uses 'know how to': 'Do you know how to operate the new cash-counting machine?'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Know operating' and 'know for operating' are not used for a skill. The original leaves out 'how', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: know how to operate

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Ramesh is **taller from his brother** by almost five centimetres.

solution.concept: A comparative adjective is followed by 'than', not 'from'
solution.explanation: Comparisons with a comparative adjective use 'than': 'Ramesh is taller than his brother by almost five centimetres.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'More taller' adds 'more' to a form that is already comparative. 'Tallest than' uses a superlative with 'than'. The original uses 'from', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: taller than his brother

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The news of her promotion **made her happily** for the whole week.

solution.concept: 'Make + object + adjective': the adjective describes the object (made her happy)
solution.explanation: After 'make + object', the word that describes the object's state is an adjective, not an adverb: 'The news of her promotion made her happy for the whole week.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Made happily her' and 'made her to be happily' keep the adverb and break the word order. The original uses the adverb 'happily', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The bank auctioned **a wooden large old cabinet** from its record room.

solution.concept: Order of adjectives before a noun: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose
solution.explanation: Size comes before age, and age before material: 'a large (size) old (age) wooden (material) cabinet'.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other orders put size after age or material before age, which breaks the normal order. The original puts the material first, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: a large old wooden cabinet

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**All what the auditor said** about the branch turned out to be true.

solution.concept: After 'all' (and 'everything', 'anything'), the relative pronoun is 'that', not 'what'
solution.explanation: 'What' already means 'the thing that', so it cannot follow 'all'. The correct form is 'All that the auditor said about the branch turned out to be true.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'That all the auditor said' turns the subject into a 'that' clause with no meaning. 'All those the auditor said' uses a plural pronoun with no noun for things said. 'All what' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: All that the auditor said

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**The manager being on leave**, the meeting was postponed to Friday.

solution.concept: Absolute phrase: a noun + participle phrase with its own subject, linked loosely to the main clause
solution.explanation: 'The manager being on leave' has its own subject ('the manager'), so it does not need to share the subject of the main clause. It means 'Because the manager was on leave'. The sentence is correct.
steps: The phrase has its own subject: 'the manager'
Absolute phrase = 'because the manager was on leave'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Being on leave' without a subject would dangle, making the meeting the one on leave. 'The manager was on leave, the meeting was postponed' joins two clauses with only a comma. 'Having on leave' drops the verb 'been'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The staff protest over the new shift timings **petered off** after the first week.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: peter out = gradually become weaker and then stop
solution.explanation: A protest that slowly lost strength and ended 'petered out'. 'Peter' is used only in this phrasal verb.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Petered down', 'petered away' and 'petered off' are not idiomatic; the verb is used only with 'out', so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
**On the wake of** the fraud, the bank introduced a second signature for large withdrawals.

solution.concept: Fixed expression: in the wake of = following, as a result of
solution.explanation: The bank acted after, and because of, the fraud. The fixed expression for this is 'in the wake of'.
steps: Meaning: following, as a result of
Fixed form: in the wake of
solution.why_others_wrong: 'At', 'by' and 'on' are not used in this expression, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.
solution.final_answer: Option B: In the wake of

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The officials behind the land scam will soon be **brought on book**.

solution.concept: Fixed expression: bring someone to book = punish them or make them answer for their actions
solution.explanation: Officials behind a scam who will be made to answer for it are 'brought to book'.
steps: Meaning: made to answer for wrongdoing
solution.why_others_wrong: 'By book', 'in book' and 'on book' are not idiomatic, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Analysts expect the effect of the one-time tax refund on spending to **wear off** within a few months.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'wear': wear off = gradually disappear (an effect, a feeling)
solution.explanation: The boost to spending from a one-time refund fades over time: it 'wears off'. The sentence is correct.
steps: Subject: the effect of a refund
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Wear out' means become useless through long use (shoes, machines). 'Wear on' means pass slowly (as the day wore on). 'Wear down' means weaken someone's resistance. None means fade.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: My uncle is a engineer in a steel plant.
My uncle is an engineer in steel plant.
My uncle is an engineer in a steel plant.
My uncle is engineer in a steel plant.

solution.concept: A singular countable noun needs an article (a/an/the) or another determiner
solution.explanation: 'Engineer' and 'plant' are singular countable nouns, so each needs an article. 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.
steps: 'an engineer in a steel plant': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The others leave out an article before 'engineer' or 'plant', or use 'a' before a vowel sound.
solution.final_answer: Option C: My uncle is an engineer in a steel plant.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: We usually go shopping on Sunday evenings.
They went for shopping in the new mall.
He went for a walk after dinner.

solution.concept: 'Go + -ing' for activities (go shopping, go swimming); 'go for + noun' (go for a walk)
solution.explanation: Activities such as shopping and swimming follow 'go' directly: 'They went shopping in the new mall.' 'Go for' is used with a noun such as 'a walk' or 'a swim'.
steps: 'went for a walk': noun after 'for': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three follow the rule: 'go' + -ing activity, or 'go for' + a noun.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They went for shopping in the new mall.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: When I was a child, I would own a bicycle.
When I was a child, I used to own a bicycle.
When I was a child, I use to own a bicycle.
When I was a child, I was used to own a bicycle.

solution.concept: 'Used to' for past states and habits; 'would' only for repeated past actions, not states such as own, have, live
solution.explanation: Owning a bicycle is a state, not a repeated action, so 'would' cannot be used. 'Used to own' describes a past state that no longer exists.
steps: 'would' is for repeated actions → wrong here
'use to' needs '-d' in a positive sentence; 'used to own': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Would own' uses 'would' with a state verb. 'Was used to own' confuses 'used to' with 'be used to' (be accustomed to). 'Use to own' drops the '-d'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: When I was a child, I used to own a bicycle.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: Here he comes with the keys.
Here comes the cashier with the keys.
There goes the last bus to the depot.
Here comes he with the keys.

solution.concept: After 'Here' or 'There' at the start, a noun subject follows the verb, but a pronoun subject comes before it
solution.explanation: With a noun subject, the verb comes first ('Here comes the cashier'). With a pronoun subject, there is no inversion: 'Here he comes', not 'Here comes he'.
steps: 'Here comes the cashier': noun subject, inverted: correct
'Here he comes': pronoun, not inverted: correct
'There goes the last bus': noun subject, inverted: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three follow the rule: the noun subjects follow the verb and the pronoun 'he' comes before it.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Here comes he with the keys.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) He watered the saplings every evening for years, even after his eyesight began to fail.
(B) The neighbours laughed and asked why a man of his age was planting trees he would never see bear fruit.
(C) At seventy, Hari Prasad dug ten pits behind his house and planted a mango sapling in each.
(D) Last summer, his grandchildren picked the first full crop and shared it with the whole lane.
(E) "These trees are not for me," he replied, "but for the children who will play under them."

solution.concept: Para jumble: named opener → reaction → reply → years of care → result
solution.explanation: C introduces Hari Prasad and the saplings. B gives the neighbours' question. E is his reply ('he replied'). A describes years of watering. D ('Last summer') gives the result.
steps: E → A (years of watering) → D (first crop): CBEAD
solution.why_others_wrong: CEBAD puts his reply before the question it answers. BCEAD opens with the neighbours laughing before anyone is introduced. CBEDA has the crop picked before the years of watering that produced it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) The women of the Lakshmi self-help group meet on the first Sunday of every month under the banyan tree.
(P) The treasurer counts the money and enters every amount in the group's register.
(Q) Members who need a loan then explain their reasons, and the group decides together whom to lend to.
(R) Each member first hands over her monthly saving of two hundred rupees to the treasurer.
(S) Once the loans are agreed, the meeting closes with a reminder of the date for repayment.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; process order marked by 'first', 'the money', 'then' and 'Once the loans are agreed'
solution.explanation: R ('first') begins the meeting with savings handed to the treasurer. P ('counts the money') follows. Q ('then') turns to loans. S ('Once the loans are agreed') closes the meeting.
steps: R → P: the treasurer counts 'the money'
solution.why_others_wrong: RQPS discusses loans before the money is counted. PRQS counts 'the money' before any is handed over. RPSQ closes the meeting once loans are agreed before any loan is discussed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) The next week, the railway office received a letter of thanks, with the money for the ticket enclosed.
(B) In a trembling voice, she explained that her purse, with the ticket inside, had been stolen at the station.
(C) An elderly woman boarded the night train to Nagpur clutching a small cloth bag.
(D) When the ticket examiner came round, she searched the bag in vain.
(E) Seeing her distress, the examiner wrote out a fresh ticket and did not charge her a fine.

solution.concept: Para jumble: named opener → problem → explanation → response → later result
solution.explanation: C introduces the woman and her bag. D: she searches the bag in vain. B explains why (the purse was stolen). E: the examiner's kind response. A ('The next week') gives the result.
steps: C → D: 'the bag' searched in vain
D → B: she explains the theft
B → E ('her distress') → A ('The next week'): CDBEA
solution.why_others_wrong: CBDEA has her explain the theft before the examiner arrives to ask for the ticket. DCBEA opens with 'she' before the woman is introduced. CDBAE puts the thank-you letter before the kindness it thanks.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) To reach them, a shopper must walk past long aisles of biscuits, snacks and soaps.
(B) Milk, bread and eggs are among the items most households buy several times a week.
(C) Many supermarkets therefore place them at the far end of the store.
(D) Along the way, many shoppers pick up things they had not planned to buy.
(E) A layout that looks inconvenient is, for the store, a carefully designed route to higher sales.

solution.concept: Para jumble: fact → decision ('therefore') → consequence ('To reach them') → effect ('Along the way') → conclusion
solution.explanation: B gives the fact that these items are bought often. C ('therefore') gives the store's decision. A ('To reach them') describes the walk. D ('Along the way') gives what happens on it. E sums up the purpose.
steps: B → C: 'therefore' placed at the far end
A → D ('Along the way') → E (conclusion): BCADE
solution.why_others_wrong: BACDE has shoppers walking 'to reach them' before the store places them anywhere. CBADE opens with 'therefore' and 'them' before the items are named. BCDAE puts 'Along the way' before the walk is described.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) When a customer deposits a cheque drawn on another bank, the money does not reach her account at once.
(P) Her bank first sends an image of the cheque through the clearing system to the bank on which it is drawn.
(Q) If everything is in order, it confirms the payment; if not, the cheque is returned unpaid.
(R) That bank checks whether the signature is genuine and whether the account holds enough money.
(S) Only after this confirmation does her bank credit the amount to her account.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; process order: 'first', 'That bank', 'If everything is in order', 'Only after this confirmation'
solution.explanation: P ('first') sends the cheque to the paying bank. R ('That bank') checks it. Q ('it confirms') gives the paying bank's decision. S ('Only after this confirmation') completes the process.
steps: (1) → P: her bank 'first' sends the image
R → Q: it confirms or returns
solution.why_others_wrong: PQRS has the payment confirmed before anything is checked. RPQS opens with 'That bank' before any other bank is mentioned. PRSQ refers to 'this confirmation' before the confirmation is described.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Ride-hailing apps do the same thing openly, raising fares when many riders want cars at once.
(B) A street vendor who sells umbrellas often raises his price the moment the rain begins.
(C) Supporters say that higher fares draw more drivers onto the roads, so that more riders get a car.
(D) Critics reply that the rise falls hardest on people who have no other way to get home.
(E) Buyers grumble, but they pay, because an umbrella is worth more to them in a downpour.

solution.concept: Para jumble: familiar example → its explanation → the same idea elsewhere ('the same thing') → defence → reply
solution.explanation: B gives the umbrella seller's price rise. E explains why buyers pay. A ('the same thing') extends the idea to ride-hailing apps. C gives the supporters' case and D the critics' reply.
steps: E → A: apps do 'the same thing'
solution.why_others_wrong: BAECD leaves the umbrella buyers' reaction until after the apps, breaking the example in two. ABECD opens with 'the same thing' before anything has been described. BEADC puts the critics' reply before the supporters' argument.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) This counter-intuitive result, in which an extra road slows a network down, is known as Braess's paradox.
(B) So many drivers took it that the roads leading to it became jammed, and average journeys grew longer.
(C) City planners once built a road linking two congested highways, expecting it to spread traffic more evenly.
(D) Some cities have since improved traffic flow by closing roads rather than building them.
(E) The new link, however, appeared to offer every driver a shortcut.

solution.concept: Para jumble: expectation → 'however' → consequence → name of the result ('This counter-intuitive result') → practical lesson
solution.explanation: C gives the plan and its expectation. E ('however') turns to what drivers saw. B ('took it') gives the jam. A ('This counter-intuitive result') names it. D ('since') draws a practical lesson.
steps: C → E: 'however', a shortcut for every driver
E → B: so many took it
solution.why_others_wrong: CBEAD has drivers take 'it' in a jam before the shortcut is explained. ECBAD opens with 'however' and 'The new link' before the road is introduced. CEABD names the result before the jam that is the result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) In a market for second-hand cars, the seller usually knows far more about a car's condition than the buyer does.
(P) Such a price is too low for the owner of a well-kept car but generous for the owner of a bad one.
(Q) As they leave, the average quality of the cars on sale falls, and buyers lower their offers still further.
(R) Unable to tell a sound car from a faulty one, buyers offer only an average price for any car.
(S) Owners of good cars, unable to get a fair price, begin to withdraw from the market.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'Such a price', 'Owners of good cars' and 'As they leave' as links
solution.explanation: R draws the consequence of (1): buyers offer an average price. P ('Such a price') explains who gains and who loses. S: owners of good cars withdraw. Q ('As they leave') gives the result, a falling average quality.
steps: (1) → R: buyers cannot tell, so they offer an average price
R → P: 'Such a price' is too low for good cars
solution.why_others_wrong: RSPQ has owners withdraw before 'Such a price' explains why. PRSQ refers to 'Such a price' before any price is mentioned. RPQS uses 'As they leave' before anyone has begun to leave.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) walked five kilometres
(Q) the old farmer
(R) to open a savings account
(S) to the bank

solution.concept: Subject + verb + distance + destination ('to the bank') + purpose ('to open ...')
solution.explanation: 'The old farmer walked five kilometres to the bank to open a savings account.' Subject (Q), verb and distance (P), destination (S), purpose (R).
steps: Destination S, then purpose R → QPSR
solution.why_others_wrong: QPRS gives 'open a savings account to the bank', which is not idiomatic. PQSR opens with a verb before its subject. QSRP puts 'to the bank' between the subject and its verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) too heavy
(Q) the box of coins was
(R) to lift
(S) for the young clerk

solution.concept: 'too + adjective + for + person + to-infinitive'
solution.explanation: 'The box of coins was too heavy for the young clerk to lift.' After 'too heavy' (P), 'for the young clerk' (S) names who cannot lift it, and 'to lift' (R) completes the pattern.
steps: 'for the young clerk' S + 'to lift' R → QPSR
solution.why_others_wrong: QRPS puts 'to lift' before 'too heavy'. QSPR puts 'for the young clerk' before 'too heavy'. PQRS opens with 'too heavy' before the subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) please call
(Q) should you need
(R) the branch helpline
(S) any help with the form

solution.concept: Inverted conditional with 'Should' (= If you need ...), then the main clause
solution.explanation: 'Should you need any help with the form, please call the branch helpline.' 'Should you need' (Q) takes its object (S); the main clause (P + R) follows.
steps: Condition: Q + S ('Should you need any help with the form')
solution.why_others_wrong: QPSR puts 'please call' between 'need' and its object. QSRP puts the object of 'call' before the verb. SQPR opens with a noun phrase that has no verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The doctor told the old man to take his medicine ______, twice a day without missing a single dose.

solution.concept: Single blank: the phrase after the comma defines the word
solution.explanation: 'Twice a day without missing a single dose' describes taking medicine at fixed times without fail: regularly.
steps: Clue: twice a day, never missing a dose
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rarely' and 'carelessly' contradict 'without missing a single dose'. 'Secretly' has nothing to do with how often the medicine is taken.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The shopkeeper ______ the price of the rice because the customer ______ to buy ten bags at once.

solution.concept: Double blank: a bulk purchase earns a discount
solution.explanation: A customer who agrees to buy ten bags at once is usually given a lower price. The shopkeeper reduced the price because the customer agreed to buy in bulk.
steps: Blank 2: buying ten bags at once → agreed
A big order earns a discount
solution.why_others_wrong: Raising the price because a customer refused to buy is illogical. Reducing it because the customer refused gives no reason for a discount. 'Hid the price' makes no sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
Whenever Meena comes across a new word in the newspaper, she ______ in her dictionary.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: look (something) up = search for information in a book or list
solution.explanation: Finding the meaning of a new word in a dictionary is 'looking it up'.
steps: Action: find its meaning in a dictionary
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Look after' means take care of. 'Look down on' means think oneself better than. 'Look forward to' means wait eagerly for. None means search in a dictionary.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The two witnesses' accounts were so ______ that the inspector could not decide which of them to believe.

solution.concept: Single blank: the 'so ... that' result decides the word
solution.explanation: The inspector cannot decide whom to believe because the accounts disagree with each other: they are contradictory.
steps: Result: cannot decide which account to believe
solution.why_others_wrong: Consistent accounts agree, so there would be nothing to decide between. 'Detailed' and 'brief' describe length, which does not explain the inspector's difficulty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The landslide left the hill village ______ for three days, with no road or telephone link to the outside world.

solution.concept: Single blank: the phrase after the comma defines the word
solution.explanation: A village with 'no road or telephone link to the outside world' is cut off from others: it is isolated.
steps: Clue: no road or telephone link
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Congested' (crowded with traffic) contradicts having no road. 'Prosperous' and 'illuminated' do not describe being cut off by a landslide.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
On the advice of his ______, the accused chose not to answer any questions until the hearing.

solution.concept: Confusable words: counsel (a lawyer; advice) vs council (an elected body) vs consul (a diplomat) vs console (comfort; a control panel)
solution.explanation: An accused person is advised by his lawyer, who is called his 'counsel'.
steps: Who advises an accused person? His lawyer
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'council' is an elected or advisory body, a 'consul' is a diplomat posted abroad, and a 'console' is a control panel (or, as a verb, to comfort). None is an accused person's lawyer.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The new manager's ______ style, in which he sought every clerk's opinion before deciding, quickly won him the ______ of the staff.

solution.concept: Double blank: a relative clause defines the first word; the result decides the second
solution.explanation: Seeking everyone's opinion before deciding is a 'consultative' style. Such a style would earn the staff's 'trust'.
steps: Blank 1: sought every clerk's opinion → consultative
Blank 2: a good style 'won him' something positive
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Autocratic' and 'arbitrary' (deciding alone or without reason) contradict asking everyone's opinion. 'Consultative ... hostility' does not fit 'won him'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
Vegetable prices ______ after the floods cut off supplies, but they returned to normal once the roads were ______.

solution.concept: Double blank: cause and effect on both sides of 'but'
solution.explanation: When supplies are cut off, prices shoot up: they 'soared'. Prices return to normal when supplies resume, that is, when the roads are 'reopened'.
steps: Blank 1: supplies cut off → prices soared
'but ... returned to normal' → supplies came back
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Slumped' (fell) does not follow from cut supplies. Prices would not return to normal once roads were 'blocked' or 'closed'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The neighbour's evidence ______ the accused's claim that he was at home that night, and the court ______ him of the charge.

solution.concept: Double blank: supporting evidence leads to a verdict of not guilty
solution.explanation: Evidence that 'corroborated' (confirmed) his alibi supports his innocence, so the court 'acquitted' him (found him not guilty).
steps: Blank 1: evidence confirming the alibi → corroborated
solution.why_others_wrong: Evidence that 'contradicted' or 'refuted' the alibi would not lead to an acquittal or clearing. 'Convicted him of the charge' clashes with evidence that supported him.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The rumour that the bank was about to close ______ to be completely false.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'turn': turn out (to be) = prove to be in the end
solution.explanation: A rumour that is shown in the end to be false 'turned out to be' false.
steps: Meaning: proved to be in the end
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Turned up' means arrived or appeared. 'Turned in' means handed over or went to bed. 'Turned over' means flipped or handed control. None is followed by 'to be' in this sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
Doctors were not sure that the injured guard would ______ after the accident, but he is now back at work.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'pull': pull through = recover from a serious illness or injury
solution.explanation: The guard survived a serious injury and is back at work: he 'pulled through'.
steps: Context: doctors unsure he would survive
He is now back at work
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Pull off' means succeed in something difficult. 'Pull over' means bring a vehicle to the side of the road. 'Pull out' means withdraw. None means recover.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The committee's ______ report, crammed with jargon and sentences that ran on for half a page, defeated even its most patient readers.

solution.concept: Single blank: the participle phrase defines the word
solution.explanation: Writing 'crammed with jargon' and with very long sentences is pompous and hard to follow: 'turgid'.
steps: Clue: jargon, sentences half a page long
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lucid' means clear. 'Terse' and 'pithy' mean short and to the point, the opposite of sentences half a page long.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The once-______ start-up, which investors had valued at several billion dollars, is now ______, its founders accused of inflating its sales.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'once' and 'now' set a past high against a present low
solution.explanation: A firm valued at billions was once highly praised: 'vaunted'. With its founders accused of inflating sales, it is now close to collapse: 'moribund'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Thriving' and 'flourishing' do not fit a firm whose founders face fraud charges. 'Obscure' and 'humble' contradict a valuation of billions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'imminent' used correctly?

options.text: He is an imminent economist who has advised three finance ministers.
She played an imminent part in setting up the village cooperative.
With dark clouds gathering over the hills, heavy rain seemed imminent.
The bank's imminent founder was honoured with a statue in the town square.

solution.concept: Imminent (about to happen) vs eminent (famous and respected) vs prominent (important, noticeable)
solution.explanation: 'Imminent' describes something about to happen. Rain that is about to fall when dark clouds gather is imminent.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three describe people or roles that are famous or important, which needs 'eminent' or 'prominent', not 'imminent'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: With dark clouds gathering over the hills, heavy rain seemed imminent.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) auditor** found that the **(B) ledger** had copied the figures wrongly into the **(C) clerk**, so the **(D) report** was delayed.

solution.concept: Word swap: check who can perform each action
solution.explanation: A ledger cannot copy figures, and figures are not copied into a clerk. Swapping B and C gives: 'The auditor found that the clerk had copied the figures wrongly into the ledger, so the report was delayed.'
solution.why_others_wrong: A-D gives 'The report found ... so the auditor was delayed', and the ledger still copies figures into a clerk. A-B gives 'The ledger found that the auditor had copied ... into the clerk'. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'enervated' used correctly?

options.text: A strong cup of tea always enervates me before a long day at the counter.
The good news enervated the staff, who cheered and danced in the hall.
Weeks of extreme heat enervated the workers, who could barely lift their tools.
The coach's rousing speech enervated the team, and they won easily.

solution.concept: Enervate = drain of energy, weaken (often misused as if it meant 'energise')
solution.explanation: 'Enervate' means to weaken or exhaust. Heat that leaves workers barely able to lift their tools has enervated them.
steps: A rousing speech that leads to a win → 'energised', not 'enervated'
Good news that makes people cheer → 'energised'
Tea before a long day → 'energises' or 'revives'
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three use 'enervate' as if it meant 'fill with energy', the opposite of its real meaning.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Weeks of extreme heat enervated the workers, who could barely lift their tools.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) lender** charged the **(B) borrower** a higher **(C) collateral** because he could not offer any **(D) interest rate**.

solution.concept: Word swap: test each bold word in its slot using banking logic
solution.explanation: A lender charges an interest rate and asks for collateral as security. A borrower who cannot offer collateral is charged a higher interest rate. Swapping C and D gives: 'The lender charged the borrower a higher interest rate because he could not offer any collateral.'
steps: An interest rate is charged, not offered
solution.why_others_wrong: A-B makes the borrower charge the lender and still has collateral being charged. B-D gives 'charged the interest rate a higher collateral', which is meaningless. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'vacate' as used in the sentence:
'The tenants were asked to vacate the flat by the end of the month so that repairs could begin.'

solution.concept: Vacate = leave a place empty, move out of it
solution.explanation: Repairs can begin only when nobody is living in the flat. To 'vacate' it is to move out and leave it empty.
steps: Purpose: so that repairs could begin
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rent', 'clean' and 'decorate' do not empty the flat, which is what the repairs need.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Benign' means gentle and not harmful, so it is close in meaning to 'harmless'. The other pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'pecuniary' as used in the sentence:
'The officer was charged with using his position to obtain a pecuniary advantage for his brother's firm.'

solution.concept: Pecuniary = relating to money
solution.explanation: Using a public position to gain something for a relative's firm is usually about money. 'Pecuniary' (from Latin 'pecunia', money) means financial.
steps: Context: an advantage for a business firm
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Political', 'legal' and 'personal' are other kinds of advantage; none is the meaning of 'pecuniary'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Ebullient' means cheerful and full of energy; 'morose' means gloomy and sullen. They are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'desultory' as used in the sentence:
'After a desultory search lasting barely ten minutes, the clerk declared that the file had been lost.'

solution.concept: Desultory = lacking a plan, purpose or enthusiasm; half-hearted
solution.explanation: A search lasting 'barely ten minutes' before giving up was done without real effort: it was half-hearted.
steps: Clue: barely ten minutes, then gave up
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Thorough' is the opposite. 'Secret' and 'urgent' are not suggested by a short search followed by giving up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Recondite' means little known or hard to understand, which is close to 'obscure'. The other pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The branch manager always keeps his desk **tidy**, with every file in its proper place.

solution.concept: Tidy = neat and in order
solution.explanation: A desk with 'every file in its proper place' is neat and orderly.
steps: Context: every file in its proper place
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Empty' contradicts the files on the desk. 'Crowded' suggests clutter. 'Wooden' describes the material, not the order.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
There has been a **rapid** rise in the number of people paying their bills by phone.

solution.concept: Rapid = happening quickly
solution.explanation: A 'rapid' rise is one that happens quickly: a fast rise.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Slight' describes a small rise, not a quick one. 'Costly' and 'planned' do not describe speed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Workers handling **hazardous** chemicals at the factory must wear gloves and masks.

solution.concept: Hazardous = risky, dangerous
solution.explanation: Chemicals that require gloves and masks are risky to handle: they are dangerous.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Expensive', 'foreign' and 'liquid' describe price, origin and form, not the danger that calls for protection.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The family's savings began to **dwindle** after two bad harvests in a row.

solution.concept: Dwindle = become gradually smaller
solution.explanation: After two bad harvests, the family must live on its savings, which gradually become smaller: they shrink.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Multiply' is the opposite. 'Stabilise' means stop changing. 'Circulate' means move around, not get smaller.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The clerk gave a **plausible** explanation for the shortage, and the manager accepted it.

solution.concept: Plausible = reasonable and likely to be true
solution.explanation: The manager accepted the explanation because it seemed reasonable and likely to be true: believable.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lengthy', 'rude' and 'written' describe length, manner or form, not whether the explanation could be believed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Shareholders were angered by the board's **pusillanimous** response to the fraud: a mild warning to the officers involved.

solution.concept: Pusillanimous = lacking courage, timid
solution.explanation: Answering a fraud with only 'a mild warning' shows a lack of courage to act firmly. 'Pusillanimous' means cowardly.
steps: Context: a fraud met with a mild warning
The board lacked the courage to act
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Decisive' is the opposite. 'Generous' and 'hasty' do not capture a fearful, weak response.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The path to the old temple is so **narrow** that two people cannot walk side by side.

solution.concept: Narrow = small from side to side; antonym: wide
solution.explanation: A path too narrow for two people side by side is small in width. The opposite is 'wide'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Steep', 'short' and 'rough' describe slope, length and surface, not width.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The branch moved out of the **dilapidated** old building, whose roof leaked every monsoon.

solution.concept: Dilapidated = in a bad condition because of age or neglect; antonym: well-maintained
solution.explanation: A building whose roof leaks every monsoon is falling apart from neglect. The opposite of 'dilapidated' is 'well-maintained'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Crumbling', 'run-down' and 'ruined' are all close in meaning to 'dilapidated'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
A **prolific** writer, she published three novels and dozens of articles every year.

solution.concept: Prolific = producing a great deal of work; antonym: unproductive
solution.explanation: Three novels and dozens of articles a year show great output. The opposite of 'prolific' is 'unproductive'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Productive' is a synonym. 'Inventive' and 'famous' describe originality and fame, not the amount produced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Losing the government contract proved **a blessing in disguise**: it forced the firm to find new customers abroad.

options.text: a gift that is given secretly
a sign of trouble to come
a misfortune that later proves useful

solution.concept: Idiom: a blessing in disguise = something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
solution.explanation: Losing the contract seemed bad, but it pushed the firm to find customers abroad, which helped it. It was a blessing in disguise.
steps: Bad at first, good in the end
solution.why_others_wrong: A secret gift reads 'disguise' literally. A sign of trouble reverses the meaning. Nothing in the sentence is a reward for honest work.
solution.final_answer: Option C: a misfortune that later proves useful

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to rest on one's laurels'.

options.text: to take a holiday after a period of hard work
to praise others for what they have achieved
to retire from a job with full honours
to be content with past success and stop trying

solution.concept: Idiom: rest on one's laurels = rely on past achievements instead of continuing to work
solution.explanation: Laurels were a symbol of victory. Someone who 'rests on his laurels' is satisfied with what he has already won and makes no further effort. For example: 'After last year's record profits, the bank cannot afford to rest on its laurels.'
steps: Resting on them = making no further effort
solution.why_others_wrong: A holiday after hard work is earned rest, not complacency. Praising others and retiring with honours are not what the idiom means.
solution.final_answer: Option D: to be content with past success and stop trying

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who cannot read or write

solution.concept: One-word substitution: education and ability
solution.explanation: An 'illiterate' person is one who cannot read or write.
steps: Key idea: unable to read or write
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ignorant' means lacking knowledge in general. 'Innocent' means not guilty. An 'amateur' does something without being paid for it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A document sent by a seller listing the goods supplied and the amount the buyer must pay

solution.concept: One-word substitution: business documents
solution.explanation: An 'invoice' lists the goods or services supplied and asks the buyer for payment.
steps: Key idea: list of goods + amount to be paid
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'receipt' confirms that payment has already been made. A 'voucher' is a document that can be exchanged for goods or that supports an entry in the accounts. A 'ledger' is a book of accounts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who is very hard to please and attentive to small details

solution.concept: One-word substitution: personality types
solution.explanation: A 'fastidious' person is very particular, demands that everything be exactly right and is hard to please.
steps: Key idea: hard to please, fussy about details
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Gregarious' means fond of company. 'Ambivalent' means having mixed feelings. 'Complacent' means too satisfied with oneself to see a need for improvement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The postman delivers the letters every morning.

options.text: The letters were delivered by the postman every morning.
The letters are being delivered by the postman every morning.
The letters is delivered by the postman every morning.
The letters are delivered by the postman every morning.

solution.concept: Simple present active → am/is/are + past participle
solution.explanation: The object 'the letters' becomes the subject. 'Delivers' (simple present) becomes 'are delivered' (plural subject), and the agent follows 'by'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Were delivered' changes the tense to the past. 'Are being delivered' is present continuous. 'Is delivered' does not agree with the plural 'letters'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The letters are delivered by the postman every morning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The bank gave him a loan of two lakh rupees.

options.text: A loan of two lakh rupees was given by him to the bank.
He was given a loan of two lakh rupees by the bank.
He has been given a loan of two lakh rupees by the bank.
He was gave a loan of two lakh rupees by the bank.

solution.concept: Verbs with two objects: the indirect object (the person) can become the passive subject
solution.explanation: 'Gave' has two objects: 'him' (the person) and 'a loan'. Making the person the subject gives 'He was given a loan of two lakh rupees by the bank.' The simple past stays simple past.
steps: Direct object 'a loan' stays after the verb
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Has been given' changes the tense. 'Was gave' uses the past tense instead of the participle. 'Given by him to the bank' reverses who gave the loan to whom.
solution.final_answer: Option B: He was given a loan of two lakh rupees by the bank.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The contractors will have completed the new branch building by June.

options.text: The new branch building will have completed by the contractors by June.
The new branch building will be completed by the contractors by June.
The new branch building would have been completed by the contractors by June.
The new branch building will have been completed by the contractors by June.

solution.concept: Future perfect active (will have + past participle) → will have been + past participle
solution.explanation: 'Will have completed' is future perfect. Its passive keeps 'will have' and adds 'been' before the participle: 'will have been completed'. 'By June' stays at the end.
steps: New subject: the new branch building
Future perfect passive: will have been + completed
Agent: by the contractors; time: by June
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Will be completed' changes the tense to simple future. 'Would have been completed' is conditional. 'Will have completed' drops 'been' and is not passive.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The new branch building will have been completed by the contractors by June.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
Meena says, "I am tired of waiting in this queue."

options.text: Meena said that she was tired of waiting in that queue.
Meena says that I am tired of waiting in this queue.
Meena says that she is tired of waiting in this queue.
Meena says that she was tired of waiting in that queue.

solution.concept: A reporting verb in the present tense ('says') does not change the tense of the reported words
solution.explanation: With 'says' (present), the tense stays as it is: 'am' remains 'is' after the pronoun change. 'I' becomes 'she'. She is still in the queue as she speaks, so 'this' can stay.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Said ... was' changes the reporting verb itself. 'Says ... was' backshifts after a present reporting verb. 'Says that I am' keeps the first person.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Meena says that she is tired of waiting in this queue.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
(Reported the next day) The clerk said, "I can open the locker now."

options.text: The clerk said that he could open the locker now.
The clerk said that he can open the locker then.
The clerk said that he could open the locker then.
The clerk told that he could open the locker then.

solution.concept: Backshift of modals (can → could) and time words (now → then) with a past reporting verb
solution.explanation: 'Said' is past, so 'can' becomes 'could'. Reported the next day, 'now' becomes 'then'. 'I' becomes 'he'.
steps: 'said that he could open the locker then'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'He can open ... then' keeps 'can'. 'Could open ... now' keeps 'now', which no longer fits a day later. 'Told that' needs an object ('told me that').
solution.final_answer: Option C: The clerk said that he could open the locker then.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Nobody except the two guards ______ allowed into the strongroom after dark.

solution.concept: A phrase beginning with 'except' (or 'but', meaning except) does not change the number of the subject
solution.explanation: The subject is 'Nobody', which is singular. 'Except the two guards' is an added phrase and does not make the subject plural: 'Nobody except the two guards is allowed ...'.
steps: 'except the two guards' does not change it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are' and 'were' agree wrongly with 'guards'. 'Have allowed' would be active and needs a plural subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Suresh is the only one of the cashiers who ______ never made a single error in ten years.

solution.concept: 'The only one of the + plural noun + who': the relative pronoun refers to 'the only one', so the verb is singular
solution.explanation: Only Suresh has never made an error, so 'who' refers to 'the only one' (Suresh), not to 'the cashiers'. The verb is singular: 'who has never made a single error'. (Compare 'one of those cashiers who have ...', where 'who' refers to the plural noun.)
steps: Present perfect with 'never ... in ten years': 'has'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Have' agrees wrongly with 'cashiers'. 'Are' and 'were' cannot be followed by 'made' to give the active present perfect.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Listen! Someone ______ at the main door of the branch.

solution.concept: Present continuous for an action happening at the moment of speaking
solution.explanation: 'Listen!' shows the action is going on right now, so the present continuous is needed: 'Someone is knocking at the main door.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Knocks' describes a habit. 'Knocked' is past. 'Has knocked' presents a completed action, which does not fit 'Listen!'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
"Why are your hands so black with grease?" "I ______ the old generator all morning."

solution.concept: Present perfect continuous for a recent, continuing activity whose result is visible now
solution.explanation: The greasy hands (present result) come from an activity that has been going on through the morning. This needs the present perfect continuous: 'I have been repairing the old generator all morning.'
steps: Activity over a period up to now: 'all morning'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Am repairing ... all morning' cannot take a duration up to now. 'Had repaired' refers to a time before another past event. 'Repair' describes a habit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
If the clerk were not so careless, he ______ the wrong account number yesterday.

solution.concept: Mixed conditional: a present unreal condition (were) with a past result (would have + past participle)
solution.explanation: 'If the clerk were not so careless' describes his general, present character. 'Yesterday' puts the result in the past, so the main clause needs 'would have + past participle': 'he would not have entered the wrong account number yesterday'.
steps: Condition: present, unreal ('were not so careless')
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Would not enter' describes a present or future result, which clashes with 'yesterday'. 'Had not entered' is the form of an 'if' clause, not a result. 'Will not have entered' is a real future form.
solution.final_answer: Option A: would not have entered

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ patience is essential for anyone who deals with customers all day.

solution.concept: Abstract nouns used in a general sense take no article
solution.explanation: 'Patience' here means patience in general, not a particular patience, so it takes no article: 'Patience is essential for anyone who deals with customers all day.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'The patience' would refer to a particular patience already mentioned. 'A' and 'an' are not used with an uncountable abstract noun in this sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Many historians believe that ______ printing press did more to spread literacy than any other invention.

solution.concept: Generic 'the' + singular countable noun to refer to an invention or type as a whole
solution.explanation: The sentence is about the printing press as an invention, not about one particular machine. A whole class or invention is referred to with 'the' + singular noun: 'the printing press'.
steps: The noun names an invention as a whole
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A printing press' would mean any single machine, which cannot have spread literacy more than other inventions. 'An' does not fit the consonant sound of 'printing'. A singular countable noun cannot stand without an article.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
She is very interested ______ learning how the share market works.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'interested in'
solution.explanation: The adjective 'interested' takes 'in': 'She is very interested in learning how the share market works.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Interested on', 'interested at' and 'interested for' are not used.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
This small town is famous ______ its handmade brass lamps.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'famous for' (the thing that makes a place or person well known)
solution.explanation: A town that is well known because of its brass lamps is 'famous for' them.
steps: Reason it is known: its brass lamps
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Famous by', 'famous with' and 'famous about' are not used for the reason something is well known.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
Under the agreement, the courier company is liable ______ any loss of documents in transit.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'liable for' = legally responsible for
solution.explanation: A company that must pay for documents lost in transit is legally responsible for the loss: 'liable for any loss'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Liable of', 'liable with' and 'liable at' are not used. ('Liable to' means likely to or subject to, as in 'liable to a fine', which is a different sense.)

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
Before the promotion interview, she decided to ______ her knowledge of foreign exchange rules.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: brush up (on) = refresh one's knowledge of something learnt earlier
solution.explanation: Before an interview, a candidate refreshes what she already knows: she 'brushes up on' her knowledge.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Brush off' and 'brush aside' mean dismiss or ignore. 'Brush past' means move quickly past someone, touching them. None means refresh knowledge.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
Leave now, ______ you will miss the last bus to the village.

solution.concept: 'Or' after an instruction = otherwise (introduces what will happen if the instruction is not followed)
solution.explanation: Missing the bus is what happens if you do not leave now. 'Or' introduces this result: 'Leave now, or you will miss the last bus.'
steps: Consequence of not leaving: miss the bus
solution.why_others_wrong: 'And' would mean that leaving now makes you miss the bus. 'But' signals a contrast that is not there. 'So' would make missing the bus the result of leaving.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ the new bridge over the river is open, villagers can reach the town in twenty minutes.

solution.concept: 'Now that' = because (something new) is now the case
solution.explanation: The bridge has just opened, and because of this the journey is now short. 'Now that' introduces a new situation as the reason.
steps: Clause 1: the bridge is now open (new situation)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Even though' signals a contrast. 'Unless' makes the open bridge a condition that blocks the result. 'In case' expresses a precaution.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ you pay in cash or by card, you will get a printed receipt for the bill.

solution.concept: 'Whether ... or' = it makes no difference which (of the alternatives)
solution.explanation: The receipt is given in both cases, cash or card. 'Whether you pay in cash or by card' means 'it does not matter which'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either ... or' cannot begin a clause that leads into a main clause this way. 'Unless' makes no sense with two alternatives. 'Although' signals a contrast, but getting a receipt does not contrast with paying.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Combine the two sentences into one without changing the meaning, and choose the option that correctly begins the combined sentence.
The bank cut its fees. It wanted to attract more young customers.

options.text: With a view to attract more young customers,
With a view of attract more young customers,
In view of attracting more young customers,
With a view to attracting more young customers,

solution.concept: 'With a view to' (= with the aim of) is followed by a gerund, because 'to' here is a preposition
solution.explanation: 'It wanted to attract more young customers' gives the bank's aim. 'With a view to attracting more young customers, the bank cut its fees.' The 'to' in 'with a view to' is a preposition, so the verb after it takes the -ing form.
steps: Relation: 'It wanted to ...' is the purpose
solution.why_others_wrong: 'With a view to attract' uses a base verb after the preposition 'to'. 'In view of' means 'considering', not 'with the aim of'. 'With a view of attract' changes the preposition and uses a base verb.
solution.final_answer: Option D: With a view to attracting more young customers,
